name: Sigstore
summary: Signing for releases, images and packages without keys to manage: a short-lived certificate tied to a login or CI job, and a public log of every signature.
intro: Sigstore replaces long-lived signing keys with identities. To sign, a client such as Cosign creates a fresh key pair and asks an OpenID Connect provider for a token that says who is signing: an email account, a cloud service account or a CI job such as a GitHub Actions workflow. Fulcio, Sigstore’s certificate authority, checks the token and issues a short-lived certificate that binds that identity to the public key. The client signs, throws the private key away, and records the artifact’s digest, the signature and the certificate in Rekor, an append-only transparency log. A verifier checks the signature, checks that the certificate names the identity it expects, for example a given repository’s release workflow, validates the certificate against Sigstore’s root of trust and confirms the entry is in Rekor.

The project runs Fulcio and Rekor as a free public-good service, generally available since October 2022 with a 99.5% uptime objective, and organisations can run their own. Cosign signs container images, storing signatures in the registry with the OCI 1.1 referrers mechanism, as well as files, SBOMs and attestations such as SLSA provenance. npm has used Sigstore for package provenance since 2023, PyPI for attestations since November 2024, and Kubernetes signs its release images and binaries with it. Rekor v2, a cheaper log built on tiles, became generally available in October 2025 while v1 went into maintenance. Sigstore graduated in the OpenSSF in March 2024; Cosign’s latest release is 3.1.4, from October 2026.
strengths: No private keys to store, rotate or lose: each key signs once and is thrown away
Verification names a person or CI workflow instead of a key fingerprint, so “built by this repository’s release job” can be checked
A free public instance already used by npm, PyPI and Kubernetes, and supported by registries such as Harbor
Every signature is in a public log, so maintainers can watch for signatures made in their name
limits: The public log is public: the signer’s identity, such as an email address, and the artifact digest are visible to anyone
Keyless signing depends on the public services being up; in February 2023 rate limits left some Kubernetes patch-release images unsigned
A signature only proves who signed: verifiers must pin the expected identity and issuer, or any valid identity passes
Rekor v2 drops the search index, signed timestamps and most entry types, so older tooling built on v1 has to change

story: Signing software usually meant generating a long-lived key, guarding it and getting users to trust it. The Linux Foundation announced Sigstore on March 9, 2021 with Red Hat, Google and Purdue University as founding members, to make signing release files, container images and binaries easier to adopt and free, with signing records kept in a public log designed to resist tampering. Luke Hinds of Red Hat said it would let “all open source communities” sign their software; Dan Lorenc of Google said it aimed “to make all releases of open source software verifiable”.

The community ran a best-effort public instance through 2021 and 2022. On October 25, 2022 Fulcio and Rekor reached 1.0 and general availability, with an uptime objective, round-the-clock on-call and a third-party audit whose findings had been fixed. Large registries followed: Kubernetes signed its images from version 1.24 in 2022, npm launched provenance in April 2023 and PyPI made attestations generally available in November 2024. Sigstore graduated in the OpenSSF in March 2024, and in October 2025 Rekor v2 moved the log to a tile-based backend to cut running costs.

choices.choice: Short-lived keys certified to an identity
choices.why: Guarding long-lived keys is the hard part of signing. Binding a throwaway key to an OIDC identity in a short-lived certificate removes key management and lets verifiers reason about who signed, not which key.

A certificate that expires soon after signing can’t be checked later on its own. Recording every signing event in Rekor proves it happened while the certificate was valid, and lets anyone audit or monitor signatures made with their identity.
Making signing as easy as running one command needed a certificate authority and log that every project could use without setting anything up, run by the community rather than a vendor.
